phase1.intro:
Alright, before we build anything, let's get your workbench set up.

There are three things you need before you can write Java with me. Where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: What do I actually need installed?
dialogue:
First up — the [[term:JDK]], the Java Development Kit. Think of it as your whole toolbox in one install.

It bundles the compiler, [[term:javac]], plus the runtime you need to actually execute what you build.

No JDK, no javac, no compiling — full stop. [[warn:A JRE alone isn't enough]] — that only runs finished programs, it can't build yours.

Once it's installed, open your terminal and check `java -version` and `javac -version`. Both need to answer before anything else here matters.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧰 your whole toolbox in one install
stickyNote.definition: Bundles the javac compiler and the runtime needed to build and run Java programs. A JRE alone can't compile code.

topics.buttonText: What should I write my code in?
dialogue:
Second — somewhere to actually write this stuff. Any text editor technically works, but you'll want an [[term:IDE]].

IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, and VS Code are the three you'll run into constantly.
[[key:IntelliJ Community Edition and VS Code are both free and won't overwhelm you on day one]] — that's genuinely where I'd start if I were you. Pick one, don't overthink it.

stickyNote.flavor: ✍️ where the toolbox actually gets used
stickyNote.definition: Integrated Development Environment — a code editor built for writing, running, and debugging programs. IntelliJ Community and VS Code are both free starting points.

topics.buttonText: Why does running code feel like two steps?
dialogue:
Third — and this one trips people up constantly, so pay attention. Building a Java program is [[key:always two separate steps, never one]].

Remember the blueprint-and-object idea? Same shape here: `javac` takes your `.java` file and turns it into `.class` bytecode — that's finishing the blueprint.
Then `java` hands that blueprint to the JVM, which actually builds and runs the thing. [[warn:Writing the code and running the code are not the same step]] — you always compile first, then run.

stickyNote.definition: javac compiles your .java file into .class bytecode; java then hands that bytecode to the JVM to run it. Compiling and running are always separate steps.

phase1.openingDialogue: Time to set up your workspace! Don't worry, I'll guide you through it step by step~ 🛠️

phase2.explanation: Nothing to break yet — we haven't written real code together. But there's a setup mistake I see constantly, so let's get ahead of it: installing a JRE instead of a full JDK, or grabbing a JDK version your IDE doesn't actually support. [[warn:No javac means no compiling, full stop]] — no matter how good your code looks, it never becomes a program without it. Run `java -version` and `javac -version` in your terminal. If `javac` isn't found, that's the JDK, not your code — fix that first.

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's check if you got the workflow right~ 🤔

mcq.question:
Quick check on the workbench workflow — what's the correct order to get a Java program running?

A) java → javac → run
B) compile → write code → run
C) javac → java
D) write code → javac → java

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: one of the IDEs I mentioned — Eclipse — has a name with a bit of a rivalry behind it. IBM built it in 2001, and according to the team's own retelling years later, the name was picked because they wanted to "eclipse" a competing tool. It's never been fully confirmed which competitor they meant, and there's long-standing debate over whether it was also a quiet dig at Sun Microsystems, since Sun made Java. Either way — someone on that team really wanted their IDE's name to throw shade.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go set up your workbench — one more thing~
